strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in 3D medical vision–language pre-training: limited paired image–report data, by combining contrastive alignment with report generation and vision-only MAE pre-training to exploit unpaired CT volumes.

Provides a systematic and extensive empirical study of CLIP-style training choices in 3D medical imaging, including report length, sentence shuffle/shortening, field of view, patch size, token aggregation, batch size, loss function, and MAE/RRG integration. The ablations yield useful practical insights.

Demonstrates strong results on global downstream tasks: classification probing, retrieval, and report generation. The clinical report-generation metrics improve substantially over baselines, and the paper reports both lexical and clinical metrics rather than only lexical overlap.

The paper is generally clear, with detailed implementation and preprocessing descriptions, public datasets, and appendix prompts. Limitations and negative results (e.g., segmentation underperformance) are discussed rather than hidden.

The proposed COLIPRI family offers a reasonable recipe for adapting CLIP to 3D medical data and shows that language-aligned representations can be competitive with or superior to prior 3D medical VLMs on global tasks.
weaknesses: The claimed zero-shot classification capability is weakened by the “native” prompting scheme, which uses 50 positive and 50 negative long reports per abnormality at test time, effectively requiring label information and report retrieval rather than performing true zero-shot classification. The true “short” prompt zero-shot setting is substantially weaker and below fVLM, so the zero-shot claims are somewhat overstated.

The methodological novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing objectives (CLIP, CapPa-style report generation, MAE) and adapts them to 3D chest CT. The contribution is more an empirical recipe and benchmark study than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Semantic segmentation does not improve over MAE pre-training and is only slightly better than training from scratch on some datasets, contradicting a strong “competitive segmentation” reading. The paper acknowledges this, but the limitation is significant because dense tasks are a major motivation for medical image understanding.

Baseline comparisons are not always fully apples-to-apples. Some baseline numbers are taken from prior work, probing/prompting setups differ, and the paper notes configuration issues for CT-CLIP; this complicates the state-of-the-art claims.

Evaluation is limited to chest CT datasets (CT-RATE, NLST, RAD-ChestCT). Despite the title’s general “3D medical image understanding” framing, there is no validation on other 3D modalities such as MRI, limiting claims of generality.

Report generation is evaluated with GPT-based metrics and GPT-4o preprocessing; absolute clinical scores remain low (e.g., RadBERT Macro-F1 around 40 and RadFact around 25), and there is no human evaluation. The reliability of the LLM-based report preprocessing and evaluation could be further scrutinized.

Some hyperparameter and preprocessing choices (e.g., fixed input size, patch size, segmentation normalization/resampling) may be suboptimal for dense tasks, and the paper does not fully resolve why the combined objectives fail to help segmentation.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic ablation of CLIP design choices for the 3D medical domain (patch size, input volume, token aggregation, batch size, augmentations), yielding concrete, transferable practical guidance (e.g., smaller input sizes and mid-sized batches with fewer iterations are preferable; sentence shuffling and short-sentence augmentation reduce the long-report/short-prompt distribution shift).

A well-motivated combination of three complementary objectives — CLIP contrastive alignment, a CapPa-style radiology report generation (RRG) objective, and a vision-only MAE objective — that lets the model exploit both paired image-report data (CT-RATE) and large unpaired datasets (NLST), with careful optimization of each component (masking ratio, decoder depth, loss weights, etc.).

Holistic and multi-faceted evaluation across global (retrieval, linear probing, zero-shot classification) and dense (semantic segmentation) tasks and several datasets (CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, LiTS, Lung, KiTS23), which is more informative than the single-metric comparisons common in this space.

Clear quantitative gains on classification probing (e.g., +2 AUPRC / +1.5 AUROC over the strong Merline baseline) and substantial improvements in clinically grounded report generation metrics (large RadBERT Macro-F1 and RadFact-CT/F1(+) gains), demonstrating that the learned embeddings capture clinically relevant semantics.
Strong reproducibility: detailed preprocessing, hyperparameters, prompting strategies, and the full GPT prompts are provided in the appendix, which is unusually thorough and useful for the community.
Honest and thoughtful limitations section that discusses negative results (segmentation, prompt sensitivity) and proposes concrete directions (e.g., iBOT-style MIM) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core ingredients (CLIP, CapPa-style captioning, MAE) are established, and the contribution is largely the systematic application and combination of these in the 3D medical setting. This is valuable but incremental relative to a new paradigm.

The combined CLIP+RRG+MAE model does not improve — and in several configurations degrades — dense segmentation performance relative to MAE-only pre-training, which undercuts the 'comprehensive' framing for dense tasks and suggests the objectives are not fully complementary.

Zero-shot classification is highly sensitive to prompt formulation (a ~7-point AUROC gap between 'native' and 'short' prompts for COLIPRI-C), limiting robustness and clinical usability of the zero-shot capability that is central to the paper's motivation.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o for report re-translation, structuring, shortening, and RadFact evaluation introduces reproducibility/cost concerns and potential bias; the evaluation depends on an external proprietary model whose behavior may change over time.

Absolute clinical report generation scores remain low (Macro-F1 around 40, RadFact-CT/F1(+) around 20), so the practical clinical significance of the reported gains is limited despite the relative improvement over baselines.

Evaluation is confined to chest CT (and abdomen-derived baselines), so generalization to other 3D modalities (MRI, etc.) is unverified, which is relevant given the broad claims about '3D medical image understanding'.

Comparability of some baselines is imperfect — several reference values are taken from other papers (e.g., fVLM excludes two abnormalities), some baseline runs failed, and probing-setup differences are acknowledged — so 'state-of-the-art' claims are only partially substantiated.

strengths: Systematic and unusually extensive ablation study over practical design axes (input size, patch size, token aggregation, batch size/iterations, loss form, augmentation strength, report length handling, prompting style), yielding concrete, transferable guidance for 3D medical vision-language pre-training.

Multi-task, multi-dataset evaluation (retrieval, linear probing, zero-shot classification, report generation, segmentation on CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, LiTS, Lung, KiTS23) is broader than typical for this subfield.

Several diagnostic findings are genuinely useful and well supported: the training/short-prompt distribution shift caused by long Findings sections, and the Sentence Shuffle + Short Sentence augmentation that mitigates text-encoder overfitting (Tab. 1, Tab. 12); the ~10-point 'native' vs 'short' prompting gap (Tab. 8, Tab. 13).
Reproducibility-oriented reporting: preprocessing, token-aggregation/probing grid search, metric definitions, and all LLM prompts are documented in the appendix (Sec. A–E).
The Limitations section candidly acknowledges prompt brittleness and the weak dense-task transfer, which is a positive practice.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. COLIPRI is a combination of existing objectives (CLIP, CapPa-style report generation, MAE), and the claim that 'no work has combined self-supervised and vision-language objectives, nor has any research in the 3D imaging domain introduced a text generation objective' is not substantiated and is contradicted by the related work the authors themselves cite for 2D (SigLIP 2, LocCa) and by existing 3D report-generation/MIM+CLIP work. The framing as an algorithmic contribution is thus misaligned with what is delivered (an ablation/best-practice study); reframing as an analysis/benchmark paper would make the contribution type coherent, but the current claims are algorithmic.

The paper's central premise—that vision-only pre-training on unpaired data (NLST) alleviates data scarcity—is not supported by its own results. The MAE objective reduces linear-probe and zero-shot performance (Sec. 6.1, Tab. 7) and yields segmentation well below MAE-only pre-training (Tab. 10: e.g., LiTS mean 80.75 for MAE vs 76.93 for COLIPRI-C). Sec. 6.6 concedes 'combining the global alignment objective with the masked image encoder objective does not synergise', which directly undercuts the 'comprehensive' inductive-bias narrative.

The headline model (COLIPRI-CRM) is generally worse than the simple optimized CLIP baseline (COLIPRI-C) on most global metrics (Tab. 6, Tab. 7), so the abstract's claim that the added inductive biases drive state-of-the-art results is not evidenced; the best configuration is essentially the ablated CLIP baseline.

State-of-the-art claims are not supported. Zero-shot classification on CT-RATE is effectively tied with fVLM (77.80 vs 77.8 AUROC) and worse on RAD-ChestCT (66.98 vs 68.0); segmentation is described as 'competitive' but is clearly inferior to MAE. The abstract's 'achieve state-of-the-art performance ... and remain competitive for semantic segmentation' overstates the evidence.

The 'native' zero-shot protocol is not zero-shot: it requires 50 labeled positive and 50 labeled negative test-time reports per abnormality to form the text embeddings (Sec. C.3). This injects test-set label information at inference and makes the primary zero-shot numbers non-comparable to standard zero-shot evaluation, including the fVLM numbers the authors compare against.

Baseline comparison protocols are inconsistent and potentially unfair. Baselines are re-run under a custom probing pipeline that the authors themselves state is 'largely superior to previous probe setups' (Sec. 6.1), inflating baseline AUROC (e.g., CT-CLIP 61.21 vs the published 75.1 in Shu et al.), while zero-shot comparisons mix re-run numbers with literature numbers (Tab. 8, Tab. 13). The reliability of the re-implemented baselines (notably CT-CLIP, which 'curiously performs worse') is never established, so the reported margins are ambiguous.

Generalization is not genuinely tested: RAD-ChestCT is derived from CT-RATE, so it is not an independent external dataset. No truly external cohort (e.g., INSPECT, BIMCV-R, or another institution) is evaluated, yet generalization/robustness claims are made.

Report-generation comparisons are not apples-to-apples. The frozen encoder is paired with a separately trained LLaVA-style decoder and Qwen2.5-1B on the same CT-RATE data, so RadBERT/RadFact gains may reflect the decoder/LLM rather than encoder quality; absolute scores remain low (~40 RadBERT macro-F1, ~20 RadFact F1(+)) and RadFact uses GPT-4o as judge, which is not a dependable clinical metric.

The segmentation protocol is under-tuned and mismatched: encoders pre-trained at 2 mm are fine-tuned on 1 mm data (an acknowledged but avoidable mismatch), nnU-Net is run for only 37.5k iterations versus the 250k recommended by the cited framework, and only 3 folds are reported. This likely understates dense-task quality and weakens the conclusion that MIM and global alignment are not complementary.

Statistical rigor is insufficient: many claimed gains fall within overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Tab. 9 RadBERT macro-F1 across COLIPRI variants; Tab. 10 segmentation), yet improvements are asserted without significance testing or multiple seeds, and the development-phase ablation numbers (Tab. 1–6) appear to be single runs on the validation split.

Reliance on GPT-4o for re-translation and report restructuring (Sec. A.2, Sec. B, Sec. E) introduces additional noise and reproducibility concerns, and Tab. 11 shows re-translation did not help; the contribution of LLM-processed text to the final numbers is not disentangled.

The text encoder is a small (110M) X-ray-pretrained BERT; the authors' own Tab. 11 shows larger text encoders behave differently, so the 'best practice' conclusions may not generalize beyond this choice.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: 3D medical vision-language pre-training under limited paired image-report data, and proposes a comprehensive framework (COLIPRI) that combines contrastive alignment, radiology report generation, masked autoencoding, and a novel Opposite Sentence Loss.

The proposed Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) is simple yet effective for bridging the training/inference gap in zero-shot classification, and the ablations show clear gains over default CLIP configurations using long reports.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, covering classification probing, zero-shot classification, report generation, retrieval, and semantic segmentation across multiple public datasets (CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, LiTS, Lung, HVS, KiTS23), with multiple baselines and detailed ablations.

The paper reports strong results on several tasks: large improvements in report-to-image retrieval over CT-CLIP, SOTA or competitive zero-shot classification and classification probing, and improved report generation clinical metrics over CT-CLIP/CT-FM/Merlin.

The appendix is thorough, providing hyperparameters, prompts, structured report examples, additional results, and implementation details, which substantially improves reproducibility and transparency.

The motivation and limitations are largely well discussed; the authors acknowledge that clinical accuracy remains below practical thresholds and that transformer encoders still lag CNN segmentation baselines.
weaknesses: The abstract and some claims overstate the segmentation contribution: while COLIPRI exceeds some pre-training baselines, it does not outperform strong CNN references such as ResEnc-L on several segmentation datasets and metrics, so the abstract's blanket claim of state-of-the-art semantic segmentation is not fully supported.

The method relies heavily on proprietary LLM preprocessing (GPT-4o) for translating, structuring, shortening, and possibly extracting findings and evaluating RadFact scores; this can introduce prompt sensitivity, cost, and reproducibility concerns, and the paper does not fully analyze the robustness of downstream results to these LLM-generated labels.

Originality is moderate: the framework mostly combines existing ideas (CLIP, MAE, report generation) with a relatively simple opposite-sentence objective; the core technical novelty is incremental, even though the empirical validation is strong.

The classification probing comparison may be overly strong because multiple aggregation schemes and learning rates are tuned on a validation set and the best probe is selected; if baselines are not given identical tuning, this could inflate the apparent advantage, and the paper could better justify fairness.

Zero-shot classification still shows a substantial gap between native long-form prompts and short prompts, and the OSL only partially closes this gap; performance remains sensitive to prompt style and abnormality distribution.

Some baselines are compared only on subsets of abnormalities (e.g., excluding Medical Material and Lymphadenopathy in the main zero-shot table), and while an extended table exists, the main comparisons can be less complete than they appear.

Report generation clinical accuracy remains low in absolute terms (~22% F1 by RadFact-CT), so the practical clinical utility is still limited despite relative gains; the limitations section should more prominently temper the abstract's claims.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in 3D medical vision-language learning: scarce paired 3D image-report data, by effectively combining paired supervision with vision-only self-supervised learning on unpaired CT volumes.

Introduces the Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) to reduce the training-inference prompt distribution shift in zero-shot medical classification; the formulation is clear and the ablations show consistent gains for short diagnostic prompts.

The empirical validation is unusually broad for a medical VLM paper: classification probing, zero-shot classification, report generation, retrieval, and semantic segmentation across CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, LiTS, Lung, HVS, and KiTS23.

The method achieves strong results, including state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot classification, report generation, and retrieval against relevant 2D and 3D baselines, and competitive segmentation performance among transformer/MAE-based encoders.

The paper includes extensive ablations on text preprocessing, augmentation, field of view, patch size, token aggregation, loss combinations, masking, and hyperparameters, which substantially support the design choices.

The manuscript is well organized, provides detailed implementation and hyperparameter tables, supplies prompts, and indicates that model weights and inference examples are available, aiding reproducibility.
Limitations are candidly discussed, including the modest benefit of radiology report generation, the remaining gap to CNN segmentation baselines, and sub-clinical report metrics.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is mostly in combining existing objectives—CLIP, MAE, report generation, and auxiliary sentence-level supervision—rather than introducing a fundamentally new architecture or learning paradigm. As a strong empirical/systems contribution this is acceptable, but the algorithmic novelty is moderate.

The radiology report generation (RRG) objective yields only slight improvements in report generation itself and can trade off against classification/zero-shot performance. Its inclusion is not fully justified as a robust, task-general gain, despite helping retrieval.

The report preprocessing relies heavily on LLM prompts (GPT-4o) to translate, restructure, and shorten reports. This introduces potential reproducibility and versioning concerns, possible bias, API dependence, and prompt sensitivity that are not comprehensively analyzed.

Segmentation results still lag behind a strong CNN baseline (nnU-Net ResEnc-L) and only match or modestly exceed MAE in some settings; the transformer encoder architecture remains a limiting factor. Clinical report metrics also remain below thresholds expected for clinical practice, as the authors note.

Pretraining is limited to chest CT (CT-RATE and NLST), and downstream evaluation is concentrated on CT tasks. Generalization to other modalities (MRI, X-ray, ultrasound), anatomies, and external health systems is not demonstrated.

Some comparisons with prior work may be affected by configuration differences, and the paper’s probing setup is deliberately stronger and more hyperparameter-tuned than prior probing protocols. This is documented and defended, but it complicates direct comparison to reported baseline numbers.

Zero-shot performance remains notably sensitive to prompt style: there is still a sizable gap between 'native' long-form prompts and short prompts, even after OSL, suggesting that the alignment problem is not fully solved.

The focus on CT and the use of NIH/UK Biobank-scale unpaired data may limit accessibility and reproducibility for groups without similar computational resources—4×A100 GPUs and large-scale preprocessing pipelines.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: 3D medical vision-language pre-training under limited paired image-report data.
Provides a comprehensive empirical study spanning classification probing, zero-shot classification, retrieval, report generation, and semantic segmentation, with extensive ablations in the appendix.
Proposes a practical multi-objective framework combining CLIP-style alignment, radiology report generation, masked autoencoding, and the new Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL).
Reports strong improvements over several baselines on multiple benchmarks and includes careful bootstrap confidence intervals and external RAD-ChestCT evaluation.
Includes a limitations section and discusses clinical/technical shortcomings, which is useful for contextualizing the results.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: most components (CLIP, MAE, report generation, self-supervised learning) are existing techniques, and OSL is a relatively straightforward sentence-level contrastive objective rather than a substantially new algorithm.

Reproducibility is a serious concern: the manuscript repeatedly says the model/code are available at a blank URL, and report preprocessing relies on proprietary GPT-4o, making exact reproduction difficult despite including prompts.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair: the authors acknowledge their probing setup is stronger than prior work, CT-CLIP performs worse in their re-evaluation, and 2D VLM baselines are adapted through slice pooling, which may understate their capabilities.

The claim of state-of-the-art performance across all tasks is overstated: segmentation gains are mixed, with some datasets decreasing under the final model, and report generation absolute clinical metrics remain low (e.g., RadFact F1 around 22%).
External validation is limited to chest/abdomen CT datasets; no MRI or other modalities, no multi-center clinical validation, and no reader study are provided, limiting generalizability claims.

The zero-shot comparison excludes two abnormalities in the main table and relies on short prompt engineering; some of the OSL benefit may come from matching training/test prompt formats rather than fully generalizable semantic alignment.
The LLM-based restructuring and shortening of radiology reports are not validated for factual consistency; hallucinations or omitted findings could bias downstream training and evaluation.

The paper does not sufficiently discuss societal/clinical deployment risks, such as automation bias or performance variation across patient subgroups, despite operating in a high-stakes medical domain.
